submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 plant-based IBS meta-analysis found a pooled peppermint-oil symptom response favoring placebo-controlled treatment, but many included studies were limited quality and larger trials remain needed.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of plant-based therapies for irritable bowel syndrome identified 60 eligible studies overall and pooled seven peppermint-oil studies. The peppermint-oil subgroup favored treatment over placebo for dichotomous symptom improvement (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.00). The authors also stated that the quality of many included studies was limited and called for further well-powered randomized trials. This supports a pooled efficacy signal while preserving important study-quality uncertainty and does not erase rigorous null primary-endpoint trials.
submissions.populationContext: Adults with IBS represented in the peppermint-oil subgroup of a broader 2026 plant-based therapy systematic review/meta-analysis.
submissions.usageContext: Oral peppermint-oil interventions pooled across eligible IBS trials; formulation differences remain relevant and the pooled estimate must not generalize to peppermint tea, aromatherapy, topical menthol, or fixed peppermint-plus-caraway products.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The review explicitly notes limited quality in many studies and a need for larger RCTs. A pooled positive signal is not evidence of uniform benefit across formulations, populations, endpoints, or individual trials. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 multicenter pediatric randomized trial found peppermint-oil capsules were not superior to placebo for the primary abdominal-pain response or adequate-relief endpoint in IBS/FAP-NOS.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 randomized controlled trial across 13 Dutch hospitals enrolled 228 children aged 8 to 18 years with irritable bowel syndrome or functional abdominal pain-not otherwise specified. After eight weeks, treatment success defined as at least 30% reduction in abdominal-pain intensity was 44.0% with peppermint-oil capsules versus 37.3% with placebo (OR 1.33, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 3.09; P=.44), and adequate relief was also not significantly different. Adverse events were mild and infrequent. This is direct pediatric null evidence for the studied capsule regimen and must not be overwritten by adult pooled estimates.
submissions.populationContext: Two hundred twenty-eight children aged 8 to 18 years with IBS or FAP-NOS treated across 13 Dutch hospitals.
submissions.usageContext: Peppermint-oil capsules containing 182 mg administered twice or three times daily by age, with protocol-defined escalation, for eight weeks. The regimen is a research exposure and not consumer dosing guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Pediatric IBS/FAP-NOS evidence must remain separate from adult IBS trials and from peppermint sweets or other formulations. Failure to outperform placebo on the primary and key secondary endpoints does not prove every peppermint preparation is ineffective. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2022 meta-analysis of 10 RCTs / 1,030 IBS patients favored peppermint oil for global symptoms and abdominal pain, while adverse events were significantly more frequent and overall evidence quality was very low.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials involving 1,030 IBS patients found pooled benefit for global IBS symptoms (RR of not improving 0.65, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.98) and abdominal pain (RR of not improving 0.76, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.93). Any adverse event was significantly more frequent with peppermint oil (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.37), and the authors rated the overall quality of evidence as very low. This finding therefore supports a positive pooled signal only when paired with low-certainty and adverse-event context and with individual rigorous null trials.
submissions.populationContext: One thousand thirty IBS patients across 10 randomized controlled trials included in the 2022 synthesis.
submissions.usageContext: Oral peppermint-oil RCTs with heterogeneous products/formulations; evidence must remain formulation-specific where release characteristics materially differ.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Very-low overall evidence quality and significantly higher adverse-event rates materially constrain certainty. Meta-analysis cannot convert reflux risk, other interaction cautions, or formulation-specific regimens into universal safety or dosing advice. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2021 Rome-IV adult randomized trial found enteric-coated peppermint oil did not significantly outperform placebo on IBS-SSS or any secondary endpoint over six weeks.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2021 six-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in adults with Rome-IV irritable bowel syndrome compared enteric-coated peppermint oil 180 mg three times daily with placebo. Both groups improved substantially from baseline, but the between-group difference in IBS Severity Scoring System change was not statistically significant (P=.97), and no secondary endpoint significantly favored peppermint oil. This rigorous null trial is first-class counterevidence to pooled positive efficacy estimates and directly contradicts a public summary that reports no disagreement.
submissions.populationContext: Adults with moderate-to-severe Rome-IV IBS at a single U.S. academic center.
submissions.usageContext: Enteric-coated peppermint oil 180 mg three times daily for six weeks; not equivalent to other release systems or non-oral preparations and not a consumer dosing recommendation.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The trial was single-center and does not prove all formulations are ineffective, but its null between-group results must remain visible alongside meta-analytic signals. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: The 190-patient PERSUADE trial found neither small-intestinal- nor ileocolonic-release peppermint oil superior to placebo on regulatory co-primary IBS endpoints, despite selected secondary symptom improvements with small-intestinal release and more mild adverse events.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The PERSUADE double-blind trial randomized 190 Rome-IV IBS patients to 182 mg small-intestinal-release peppermint oil, 182 mg ileocolonic-release peppermint oil, or placebo for eight weeks, with 189 included in intention-to-treat analysis. Neither peppermint formulation significantly improved the FDA-style abdominal-pain response or EMA-style overall-relief co-primary endpoints versus placebo. Small-intestinal-release peppermint oil did improve selected secondary abdominal-pain, discomfort, and IBS-severity measures, while adverse events were mild but more common in both peppermint-oil groups. The trial is therefore mixed evidence with a strong formulation and endpoint boundary, not a simple positive or negative result.
submissions.populationContext: One hundred ninety adults with Rome-IV IBS randomized across four Dutch hospitals; 189 included in intention-to-treat analysis.
submissions.usageContext: Small-intestinal-release versus ileocolonic-release peppermint oil, each 182 mg for eight weeks. Release systems are distinct interventions and neither trial regimen is generic consumer dosing guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Null regulatory co-primary endpoints must remain visible alongside positive secondary outcomes. Small-intestinal-release results cannot transfer to ileocolonic-release or arbitrary enteric products, and mild adverse-event excess remains part of the evidence balance. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.
